scope: Bounded proposals for ordinary-language text only. These are not approved translations and must not be wired into a learner deck before fluent-speaker review.

candidates.sourceEnglish: Watch one bee move from one blossom to another.
candidates.candidate: Vhonani ṋotshi nthihi i tshi bva kha luvha i tshi ya kha ḽiṅwe.
candidates.backTranslation: Watch one bee go from one flower to another.
candidates.drift: Low based on this source-blind back-translation. The English verb 'move' became 'go'; the number and one-flower-to-another relationship remain. 'Blossom' is rendered as the more general 'flower'.
candidates.holdReason: The sentence is observational, not animal-care or hive-safety advice. Keep it unapproved pending a Tshivenda first-language review, including noun-class and idiomatic wording.

candidates.sourceEnglish: Bees can carry pollen as they visit flowers.
candidates.candidate: Dziṋotshi dzi nga hwala pollen musi dzi tshi dalela maluvha.
candidates.backTranslation: Bees can carry pollen when they visit flowers.
candidates.drift: No material drift identified in the back-translation. 'Pollen' remains English because a technical term should not be guessed at.
candidates.holdReason: This is a general explanatory statement, not a care instruction or safety claim. The English technical term is intentionally retained; have a Tshivenda speaker confirm whether it is understandable or has a locally preferred term.

candidates.sourceEnglish: Small livestock integration turns chickens, ducks, and bees into working parts of the farm.
candidates.candidate: U ṱanganya zwifuwo zwiṱuku zwi ngaho chickens, ducks na bees zwi ita uri zwi shume na kha purasi.
candidates.backTranslation: Joining small animals such as chickens, ducks and bees makes them work on the farm too.
candidates.drift: Low apparent drift: the three named animal groups and the idea of becoming useful parts of the farm remain. “Small livestock integration” is simplified to “joining small animals”; confirm that this is a suitable course-level wording.
candidates.holdReason: Unreviewed machine draft for Rory-authorized visible review. Keep out of a learner release until the facilitator feedback gate; check terminology, grammar, species names and local register.

candidates.sourceEnglish: Learn how animals can control pests, build fertility, support pollination, and return value to the soil.
candidates.candidate: Gudani uri zwifuwo zwi nga langa pests, zwa engedza soil fertility, zwa thusa pollination, na u vhuedzedza ndeme mavuni.
candidates.backTranslation: Learn that animals can manage pests, increase soil fertility, help pollination, and return value to the soil.
candidates.drift: Low apparent drift in the proposition. The technical terms “pests,” “soil fertility,” and “pollination” stay English for review; “control” is softened to “manage,” so confirm that the claim is not weakened too far.
candidates.holdReason: Unreviewed machine draft for Rory-authorized visible review. Keep out of a learner release until the facilitator feedback gate; check terminology, grammar, species names and local register.

candidates.sourceEnglish: Small livestock can do work beyond producing meat, eggs, or honey.
candidates.candidate: Zwifuwo zwiṱuku zwi nga ita mishumo iṅwe nga nnḓa ha u bveledza nyama, eggs kana honey.
candidates.backTranslation: Small livestock can do other work besides producing meat, eggs or honey.
candidates.drift: Low apparent drift. Product names stay exact in English except meat; check the naturalness and class agreement of the mixed sentence.
candidates.holdReason: Unreviewed machine draft for Rory-authorized visible review. Keep out of a learner release until the facilitator feedback gate; check terminology, grammar, species names and local register.

candidates.sourceEnglish: Chickens eat some insects and weed seeds.
candidates.candidate: Chickens dziḽa dziṅwe insects na seeds dza weeds.
candidates.backTranslation: Chickens eat some insects and seeds from weeds.
candidates.drift: Low apparent drift. “Some” remains; species name is retained in English to avoid an uncertain local bird term.
candidates.holdReason: Unreviewed machine draft for Rory-authorized visible review. Keep out of a learner release until the facilitator feedback gate; check terminology, grammar, species names and local register.

candidates.sourceEnglish: Ducks scratch less than chickens, but can still damage plants.
candidates.candidate: Ducks dzi ṱharamudza fhasi nga zwiṱuku u fhira chickens, fhedzi dzi nga kha ḓi tshinya zwimela.
candidates.backTranslation: Ducks scratch the ground less than chickens, but can still damage plants.
candidates.drift: Low apparent drift; comparative direction and damage possibility remain. Animal behavior wording needs fluent review.
candidates.holdReason: Unreviewed machine draft for Rory-authorized visible review. Keep out of a learner release until the facilitator feedback gate; check terminology, grammar, species names and local register.

candidates.sourceEnglish: Bees and other pollinators help many crops.
candidates.candidate: Bees na dziṅwe pollinators dzi thusa zwimela zwinzhi.
candidates.backTranslation: Bees and other pollinators help many crops.
candidates.drift: No apparent proposition drift; the technical word “pollinators” stays English.
candidates.holdReason: Unreviewed machine draft for Rory-authorized visible review. Keep out of a learner release until the facilitator feedback gate; check terminology, grammar, species names and local register.

candidates.sourceEnglish: By the end of this module, you will understand how chickens, ducks, bees, and guinea fowl fit into a working system.
candidates.candidate: Musi module iyi i tshi fhela, ni ḓo pfesesa uri chickens, ducks, bees na guinea fowl zwi shuma hani kha sisiteme i shumaho.
candidates.backTranslation: When this module ends, you will understand how chickens, ducks, bees and guinea fowl work in a functioning system.
candidates.drift: Low apparent drift; all four animal names are preserved. “Fit into” is expressed as “work in”; validate that this does not imply a stronger performance claim.
candidates.holdReason: Unreviewed machine draft for Rory-authorized visible review. Keep out of a learner release until the facilitator feedback gate; check terminology, grammar, species names and local register.

candidates.sourceEnglish: Watch the hens peck at the ground among dry plant remains.
candidates.candidate: Sedzani hens dzi tshi runga fhasi vhukati ha masalela a zwimela o omileyo.
candidates.backTranslation: Watch hens peck the ground among dry plant remains.
candidates.drift: Low apparent drift; observation, animals and dry remains are retained. Confirm the verb chosen for pecking and the spelling/spacing.
candidates.holdReason: Unreviewed machine draft for Rory-authorized visible review. Keep out of a learner release until the facilitator feedback gate; check terminology, grammar, species names and local register.

candidates.sourceEnglish: They scratch through plant remains and eat some insects and weed seeds.
candidates.candidate: Dzi runga vhukati ha masalela a zwimela nahone dziḽa dziṅwe insects na seeds dza weeds.
candidates.backTranslation: They scratch among plant remains and eat some insects and weed seeds.
candidates.drift: Low apparent drift; “some” and both food categories remain. Species subject is inherited from the exact adjacent English source; verify whether the standalone clause needs an explicit subject.
candidates.holdReason: Unreviewed machine draft for Rory-authorized visible review. Keep out of a learner release until the facilitator feedback gate; check terminology, grammar, species names and local register.

candidates.sourceEnglish: Ducks eat slugs and snails without the heavy scratching of chickens.
candidates.candidate: Ducks dziḽa slugs na snails, fhedzi a dzi runga fhasi nga maanḓa u fana na chickens.
candidates.backTranslation: Ducks eat slugs and snails, but do not scratch the ground heavily like chickens.
candidates.drift: Potential drift: “without the heavy scratching” is restated as a contrast with chickens; check the exact degree and implied behavior with a speaker. Pest names and the comparison are retained in English where useful.
candidates.holdReason: Unreviewed machine draft for Rory-authorized visible review. Keep out of a learner release until the facilitator feedback gate; check terminology, grammar, species names and local register.

candidates.drift: Low based on this source-blind back-translation. 'Watch' becomes 'look at'; the source's movement and singular count remain. 'Blossom' is rendered as the more general 'flower'.
candidates.holdReason: The sentence is observational, not animal-care or hive-safety advice. Keep it unapproved pending fluent standard-Xitsonga and local-register review. Standard written Xitsonga has not been comprehension-tested with Shangani-speaking learners.

The English technical term is intentionally retained; have a fluent Xitsonga speaker confirm whether it is understandable or has a locally preferred term. Standard written Xitsonga has not been comprehension-tested with Shangani-speaking learners.

candidates.backTranslation: Combining small livestock such as chickens, ducks and bees makes them work together with the farm.
candidates.drift: Low apparent drift: the three animal groups and farm role remain. The technical heading concept is simplified to “combining small livestock”; confirm idiomatic phrasing.
candidates.holdReason: Unreviewed machine draft for Rory-authorized visible review. Keep out of a learner release until the facilitator feedback gate; check terminology, grammar, species names and local register.

candidates.sourceEnglish: Learn how animals can control pests, build fertility, support pollination, and return value to the soil.

candidates.backTranslation: Learn how animals can manage pests, improve soil fertility, help pollination and return value to the soil.
candidates.drift: Low apparent drift in the proposition. “Pests,” “soil fertility,” and “pollination” remain English technical terms; fluent review should confirm the framing and whether “manage” captures “control.”
candidates.holdReason: Unreviewed machine draft for Rory-authorized visible review. Keep out of a learner release until the facilitator feedback gate; check terminology, grammar, species names and local register.

candidates.backTranslation: Chickens eat some insects and weed seeds.

candidates.holdReason: Unreviewed machine draft for Rory-authorized visible review. Keep out of a learner release until the facilitator feedback gate; check terminology, grammar, species names and local register.

candidates.sourceEnglish: Bees and other pollinators help many crops.

candidates.drift: Possible wording drift: “pollinators” is explained rather than named, and the repeated “help” is awkward. Meaning is preserved but requires a fluent edit; “pollination” remains English.
candidates.holdReason: Unreviewed machine draft for Rory-authorized visible review. Keep out of a learner release until the facilitator feedback gate; check terminology, grammar, species names and local register.

excludedText.slides: Slides 9-20, except the existing separately recorded candidates on slides 2 and 17 and the slide 9 candidates in this packet
excludedText.reason: This packet now drafts ordinary-language descriptive clauses on slides 1-8, excluding existing Xitsonga slide 2 copy to avoid duplication. Care, hive safety/placement, manure, crop-protection, site-specific actions, technical concepts and quantities remain exact English; see heldClausesSlides1to8 for each retained clause and reason.

backTranslationMethod: For every newly added candidate, the target wording was read without its English source and rendered back into plain English. The resulting paraphrase and any suspected meaning change are recorded beside the exact source. This is an internal drift check, not an independent speaker review.

lexicalChecks.note: Used only as a basic lexical cross-check for 'look' and 'flower'; it does not validate sentence grammar, register or meaning.
Department of Basic Education Xitsonga home-language material uses these bee/flower forms in a pollination lesson; this does not validate these candidate sentences.
A Tshivenda-English reference was identified, but no full phrase validation was available for this draft. A fluent speaker must validate every Tshivenda line.
